acv.quote: Ninety-five K ACV, on a two-year term.

header.tag_why: The CFO decided on a controller's one-pager comparing only our rate with the bank's rate, with nothing from us on what the failing orders cost Fernbrook, so the money question was settled without any value on the page.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: For buyers who come to us with their own checkout-failure numbers: 'Here's what your 'orders dying at the last step' are worth.' Put a dollar figure on their failed orders from their own decline data, starting with 'the big baskets', and use the average uplift as supporting detail only, never as the headline.
messaging_changes.why: We led with 'the average improvement in acceptance' while the champion's own data showed about one in twelve orders failing, mostly on big baskets, and the decider still read our offer as 'the same thing', so the claim needs to be the customer's lost revenue rather than our average.

messaging_changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
messaging_changes.change: Present ROI as something we calculate for them rather than cite: 'Send us three months of your declines and we'll give you a one-page business case you can hand to finance.' The page should show the value of their failed orders next to our price, and it becomes the default reply whenever a champion asks for something to give a CFO who won't take vendor meetings.
messaging_changes.why: The champion asked for 'a one-page business case' to give the CFO, and our SE offered to value the failed orders from a three-month export, but we sent the deck and pricing instead, so the CFO decided on a rate-only page with 'Nothing from us' on value.

messaging_changes.change: Add a counter-line for deals where the incumbent bank answers with a rate cut: a lower rate doesn't fix the orders that still fail at checkout, so compare the rate saving with what those failed orders cost. Use it to bring the conversation back to declines, not to negotiate the rate.
messaging_changes.why: Before the bank 'sharpened the rate', the champion was asking why big orders fail, and afterward 'every email was the rate', even though the processor never explained the failures. We have no line that brings the conversation back to that unsolved problem.

trigger.insight: The evaluation started with lost revenue that the customer measured on their own dashboard: failed orders that were concentrated in the highest-value baskets. That was a ready-made business case, and nobody converted it into dollars. By the end, a revenue problem had been reframed as a processing-cost line item.
trigger.messaging: When a prospect brings their own decline rate, translate it into lost revenue on their high-value orders within the first week, and make that figure the anchor of the pitch instead of the average uplift.

decider.insight: Finance was the only gate. IT's support was conditional on finance approving, and the CFO never met us. Our whole case therefore reached him through Lucy and a controller-built page, and we gave Lucy nothing that spoke finance. The rep assumes Lucy relayed the cost of the failed orders, but whether she did is unknown.
decider.messaging: When the decider won't take vendor meetings, our message has to travel without us: give the champion a one-page, CFO-ready asset in the customer's numbers that she can present as her own.

competitor.insight: By Lucy's account, the bank did nothing about the declines that started the evaluation. It cut its rate, and that was enough to move the conversation from the incumbent's weakness (failures it could not explain) to its strength (price). The rep's own lesson, more room on the rate, accepts the bank's framing instead of pulling the conversation back to failed orders.
competitor.messaging: When an incumbent bank answers with a rate cut, respond by restating the unsolved problem in money ('a better rate on the orders that still fail'), not by negotiating the rate line.

message.insight: The decline explanation landed with the champion, but the rep dodged the silence question. The real silence was the CFO: the M4 average-uplift message persuaded someone who was already sold and never reached the person who said no. Success measured by Lucy's nodding hid that our strongest material was never shown to the decider.
message.messaging: Replace the average-uplift claim (M4) with 'here is what your failed orders are worth', using the customer's own decline data, and position M6 ROI as something we calculate for them rather than cite.

decided.insight: The deal was decided by a document we did not write: a rate-versus-rate page with only our quote on it. Seen that way, 'the same thing' is a reasonable conclusion. Lucy's 'formality' read shows the champion misjudged the CFO, and the rep relied on her read. The CFO's line reaches us in two different wordings, both secondhand, so it is a paraphrase in spirit even though it was relayed as a quote.
decided.messaging: Make sure the decider's comparison page includes the cost of doing nothing (failed orders, plus any gateway and chargeback costs the customer confirms), so that 'the same thing' cannot survive the page.

gaps.insight: This was not a product gap. It was a proof gap we created ourselves. The champion asked for exactly the asset that would have reached the CFO, our SE offered to build it, and we skipped it to protect quarter-end timing, sending generic customer stories and an average uplift instead. Beyond the rate, the rep also mentions a gateway fee and a dedicated chargebacks person, but these are the rep's claims, and nothing from us put them on the page.
gaps.messaging: Build a standard one-page business-case template (failed-order value from a three-month export, plus customer-confirmed fees and labor) and make it the default reply whenever a champion asks for 'something to hand' finance.

language.insight: The champion talked about lost sales on expensive items ('orders dying at the last step', 'the big baskets'), while we talked about authorization rates and acceptance uplift. That vocabulary gap let the CFO hear 'the same thing'. His words show that our differentiation never made it into his language at all.
language.messaging: Use the customer's words in the business case and decks, for example 'orders dying at the last step' on 'the big baskets', each with a dollar figure attached, instead of 'authorization rate uplift'.

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam: which of our materials went to Martin, and did anything in the deck get no response from Lucy or the controller?

gaps.question: What did Martin have in front of him about what the failing orders were costing?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy (via Sam): did you present the one-in-twelve failure rate or any cost of the failed orders to Martin, and how did he react?

gaps.question: If we had matched the price, would we have won? What else would have needed to be true?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam: how far apart were our quote and the bank's sharpened rate, and how much did the IT lead's worry about moving before spring weigh with Martin?

gaps.question: How big was the gap between our rate and the bank's new rate?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam for the per-transaction figures on the controller's one-pager, if Lucy shared them.

close.rep_takeaway: When the decider won't meet you, the champion's request for 'something she could hand' finance is your only seat in that room. Take the SE's offer to run the customer's declines even at quarter-end, because a rate-only page will always read as 'the same thing', and more room on the rate does not fix that.
